questions.question: Which of the following is a characteristic that indicates a software system’s ability to perform its intended functions without failure, especially in safety‑critical environments?
questions.explanation:
Reliability is highlighted as a key characteristic for critical software where a higher level of confidence is required [Page 37].

---

questions.question: According to the context, what does the “completeness check” ensure in a requirements document?

options.A: That all design diagrams are included
options.B: That there are no contradictory constraints
options.C: That every function and constraint intended by the user is defined
options.D: That the document follows a standard template

questions.explanation:
Completeness checks verify that the requirements document includes all functions and constraints intended by the system user [Page 29].

---

questions.question: Which statement best explains the difference between verification and validation as described in the text?

options.A: Verification checks that the software meets user expectations, while validation checks code syntax.
options.B: Verification ensures the software meets its specification; validation ensures it meets the customer’s expectations.
options.C: Verification is performed only after testing, whereas validation occurs before coding.
options.D: Verification focuses on performance, while validation focuses on security.

questions.explanation:
Verification checks conformity to specifications; validation ensures the software meets customer expectations [Page 37].

---

questions.question: In the context of custom software, what testing practice is recommended to demonstrate that the software meets its requirements?

options.A: Conduct a single integration test covering all modules.
options.B: Perform at least one test for every requirement in the requirements document.
options.C: Use only automated tests without manual review.
options.D: Test only the most critical features identified by the developer.

questions.explanation:
For custom software, there should be at least one test for each requirement to show the software meets its requirements [Page 36].

---

questions.question: Which of the following best describes a “consistency check” in a requirements document?

options.A: Verifying that the document uses consistent terminology throughout.
options.B: Ensuring that no two requirements conflict or describe the same function differently.
options.C: Checking that all stakeholder signatures are present.
options.D: Confirming that the document is formatted according to the company style guide.

questions.explanation:
Consistency checks ensure requirements do not conflict or give contradictory descriptions of the same function [Page 29].

---

questions.question: Why might users have low expectations of software quality according to the provided material?

options.A: Because modern software is always free and therefore less reliable.
options.B: Because of previous experiences with buggy, unreliable software.
options.C: Because developers rarely perform validation activities.
options.D: Because testing is limited to unit tests only.

questions.explanation:
Users’ low expectations stem from past experiences with buggy, unreliable software [Page 37].

---

questions.question: Which characteristic is most directly linked to the statement “The more critical the software, the more important it is that it is reliable”?
questions.explanation:
The passage ties criticality of software to the need for higher reliability [Page 37].

---

questions.question: Which of the following actions is part of the validation process as described?

options.A: Checking that source code follows naming conventions.
options.B: Demonstrating to the developer and the customer that the software meets its requirements.
options.C: Performing static analysis to detect syntax errors.
options.D: Ensuring that every class has at least one unit test.

questions.explanation:
Validation includes demonstrating to stakeholders that the software meets its requirements [Page 36].

---

questions.question: When preparing a requirements document for an in‑house software product, the focus is primarily on:

options.A: Detailed architectural diagrams and low‑level design.
options.B: Defining user requirements and high‑level, non‑functional system requirements.
options.C: Listing every possible test case for each module.
options.D: Including exhaustive legal and regulatory compliance sections.

questions.explanation:
In‑house documents concentrate on user requirements and high‑level non‑functional requirements [Page 28].

---

questions.question: Which set of characteristics together best represent “good software” according to the themes in the context?

options.D: Color Scheme, Font Choice, Layout, Branding

questions.explanation: The text emphasizes reliability, consistency checks, completeness checks, and validation as key desirable qualities of software [Pages 29, 37].
